When we release the static site, we first upload every new asset (JS, CSS, images) under a new versioned filename, such as `app.3f9c2a.js`. Only after all of them are uploaded do we switch the manifest so it points to those new names. We leave the old assets in place.

The upload comes before the switch because the manifest is what tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it first, a browser could read the new manifest and request files that don't exist yet. That browser would get 404s and a broken page. When everything is uploaded first, every name in the new manifest already resolves when browsers start using it.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that are already running the site. A user who loaded the page before the switch still has the previous manifest, and that browser will keep requesting the old filenames, for example when it lazy-loads a route or fetches a chunk. If we deleted those files, those sessions would break partway through. Because the old files stay available, those users keep a working page, and they pick up the new version the next time they load the manifest.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names. The manifest is the only thing that tells a browser which asset files to load, so changing it is what actually makes the release live.

The upload comes first so that every name in the new manifest already exists when browsers start reading it. If we switched the manifest first, a browser could fetch the new manifest and request a file that hasn't arrived yet, which gives a 404 and a broken page. Because new assets use new names, uploading them changes nothing that users see. Nothing references them until the manifest switch, so the switch is the single moment the release takes effect.

We keep the old assets because browsers that fetched the previous manifest still have it in memory or cache, and they will keep requesting the old filenames. A tab opened before the release might lazy-load a script or stylesheet minutes or hours later. If we deleted the old files, those requests would fail and the page would break partway through use. Versioned names let old and new files exist side by side without overwriting each other. Each browser gets the matching set for whichever manifest it loaded, so no one receives a mix of old and new code.

This also makes rollback simple. Pointing the manifest back at the previous names restores the old release immediately, because those files are still in place.

A release has two steps: first we upload every new asset under a versioned name (for example `app.3f9c2e.js`), then we switch the manifest to point at those names. The manifest is the only file that changes meaning between releases. Every asset name refers to exactly one version of its content and never changes.

The upload comes before the switch so the manifest never points at a file that isn't there yet. Once the new manifest is live, any browser can fetch it right away and immediately request the assets it lists. If those assets were still uploading, the browser would get 404s or half-written files and render a broken page. When we upload first and confirm the files, the switch becomes a single, near-instant change. Before it, everyone gets the old release. After it, everyone gets the complete new release. Nobody sees a mix of the two.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. A user who opened the site a minute before the release still has the old manifest in memory. As they navigate, that page keeps requesting old asset names, including lazy-loaded chunks, route bundles, fonts and images. If we deleted those files at release time, their session would break partway through, often as a failed chunk load or a blank section. CDN and browser caches can also keep serving the old manifest for a while. Keeping the old assets lets those sessions finish on the version they started with, and the next full page load picks up the new manifest.

Versioned names are what make both steps safe. Old and new files never share a name, so uploading the new release can't overwrite anything an existing session depends on. Since each name always maps to the same content, assets can also be cached aggressively.
